startingActivity.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order
learnerActions: Hold a real cube and turn it in your hands.
Count the faces first: colour or number each flat surface as you touch it, saying 'face' each time, until every face is marked. Record the total.
Then trace each edge with a finger, marking each traced edge (e.g. a gold line or sticker), saying 'edge' each time, until all are traced. Record the total.
Then dot each vertex (corner) with a sticker, saying 'vertex' each time. Record the total.
Recount starting from a different face to check your totals stay the same (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A face, an edge and a vertex are three different things; counting each property separately in a fixed order, and marking features as you go, keeps them distinct and makes sure nothing hidden is missed or double-counted.

startingActivity.title: Predict then fold: does this arrangement close into a cube?
learnerActions: Look at a flat arrangement of six squares and, before folding, commit to a prediction: 'will this fold into a closed cube?' and say WHY.

Fold the staircase and observe that it ALSO closes into a cube, with every face covered once and no face left open (allowing for slight gaps from card thickness).

Physical card/Polydron cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held, but they stand in for ideal flat (zero-thickness) faces; frame questions around the mathematical net and the cube it would fold into, not around whether the physical card can be picked up.

The 'line of four squares' composite applies to nets that contain such a line (e.g. the cross/1-4-1); it is not present in every valid net (e.g. the 2-2-2 staircase), where the general strategy is to track each square's destination from the base.

Supporting non-standard nets on screen or in card lets 'only the T-net works' be disproved directly.

A 'which of these fold into a cube?' selection question is a useful CHECK after folding work; include a valid non-prototype net and an invalid six-square block as options. Recognition-only selection does not by itself elicit the folding reasoning or the production of a new net — pair it with asking the child to name opposite faces or draw a new valid net.
Spoken explanation of a prediction is a valuable prompt but is not a substitute for the spatial folding itself.

Apply a length comparison (e.g. a ruler lens or measuring them against each other): name the taller as the winner — 'taller'.
Apply a weight comparison (e.g. a balance that tips to the heavier): name which is heavier.

Apply a capacity comparison: fill the tall bottle to the top and pour it into the wide jar; if the jar takes it all with room to spare it holds more. Choose containers where the pour really shows this, and let the actual result stand.
Say aloud which object wins for each attribute, using the matching comparative word.
Notice that the same two objects can win on different attributes, so there is no single answer to 'which is bigger?'

Counterexample outcomes (big ball lighter than small stone; tall glass vs wide bowl) depend on the specific objects chosen; pick objects that reliably produce the intended contrast and confirm by weighing or pouring rather than asserting.

startingActivity.title: Measuring station: choose the tool and the unit
learnerActions: Set out a mixed set of objects one at a time — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if available, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler/tape, a kitchen scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer all available.
For each object, first say out loud what KIND of measurement this is: how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?
Pick the matching instrument, then choose the standard unit (m or cm, kg or g, litres or ml, °C).
Measure to the nearest mark and state the amount with its unit.

Try a deliberate mismatch — measure the pencil in metres — and notice the number is useless (to the nearest metre a pencil rounds to '0 m'); then switch to centimetres and get a clean reading (a real pencil is usually somewhere between about 10 cm and 19 cm, depending on how much it has been sharpened).
Try reaching for the ruler to measure the jug of juice and notice it cannot give a capacity reading at all.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: You first decide what kind of quantity you are measuring so the unit family and tool fit, then choose a unit grain that gives a sensible, readable number.

A reference card reminds learners of benchmarks but cannot let them make and test a choice; it is a scaffold, not the core activity.
Assessment is best done by watching the learner choose the tool and unit across a mixed set of objects, not by asking them to recite rules.
An interactive live-recompute station is one way to make a bad grain visibly awkward; real instruments and objects achieve the same learning and should not be treated as replaceable by a screen only.

Choosing units is primarily a categorical/attribute judgement; a spatial 3D setting may offer little specific additional leverage for it, and in-role dialogue can discuss but not itself rehearse the watched act of picking a tool — these are observations about fit, not claims that any medium is necessary or impossible.

startingActivity.title: Build a fair three-colour spinner and test it by sampling
learnerActions: Try to divide a spinner into three colours (red, blue, green) so that each colour is equally likely to be landed on.
Spin the spinner many times (e.g. 100 times) and keep a tally of how often each colour comes up.

If one colour comes up clearly more often over many spins, examine the spinner: is one wedge bigger than the others? (Small differences in the tally can happen by chance even on a fair spinner.) Adjust the boundaries until the three wedges are the same size, checking the sizes directly, then spin and tally again.
State in your own words what makes the three colours equally likely — the equal AREA of each section, not the fact that there are three colours.
Then build the opposite: a cube with 1 red face and 5 blue faces (six equal faces), or a spinner split into six equal sections with 1 red and 5 blue; predict and then tally the long-run result.
Compare your prediction with the tally and explain why two colours did NOT give a 50-50 result.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Equal chance depends on each outcome region being the same size (or the same number of equal ways), not on how many different outcomes there are; sampling many times reveals equal-area regions producing roughly equal frequencies and unequal regions producing a lopsided tally.

startingActivity.title: Balance beam: build both sides and watch it level
learnerActions: Set an expression on the left pan and another on the right (for example 5+2 on the left, 6+1 on the right) using identical cubes on a physical pan balance (5 cubes and 2 cubes on one side, 6 cubes and 1 cube on the other), or number/operation tiles on an on-screen balance that weighs each side by its value.
Predict whether the beam will tip or settle level, and say why, before releasing it.
Watch whether the beam tips or settles level: with identical cubes (or an on-screen balance that weighs by value), it sits level only when both sides share the same value.
Try a case where the sides look different but balance: put 8 on the left and 5+3 on the right and observe that the beam still sits level.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: The equals sign is the pivot/balance point: two sides are equal when they share the same value, regardless of how each side looks or which side 'the answer' is on. '=' is not a direction to compute leftward.

learnerActions: Set out an equation with a box, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, on a two-pan balance or bar model where one side already shows 5.

startingActivity.title: The 'convince me' partner
learnerActions: Pose the child a within-20 calculation (e.g. 8 + 5) and ask them to explain HOW they worked it out.
Then ask 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'.
When the child stalls or only asserts ('I just know', 'I reckon it's right'), hand over a sentence stem: 'Start with because…' and prompt for the missing link.
Have the child upgrade a confident hunch into a chain, e.g. 'because 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10, so 10 and 3 more is 13'.
Ask the child to show the same calculation a different way and check whether it also gives the answer ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?').
Present a worked example containing a slip (e.g. a number bond that doesn't actually make ten) and ask 'Is this right? How can you tell?' — pushing for WHICH step is wrong and WHY.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A confident answer is not the same as a justification; a reason that works can be built by linking steps with 'because' and 'so', and an alternative method that agrees is supporting evidence that backs up the reason, though it does not replace explaining why.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: When there are endlessly many cases, as with even numbers, no pile of examples can establish a claim for every case, but a structural reason can — and a single counter-example is enough to disprove a general ('always') statement even though many examples cannot prove one.
